Summary\\n\\nAdd an opt-out Razor compile-time transformation that rewrites literal `~/...` static asset paths into equivalent `Assets[\\\"...\\\"]` expressions for explicitly opted-in component parameters and a conservative set of HTML attributes.\\n\\nRuntime assemblies only provide metadata attributes and built-in declarations for Razor to discover. No runtime code inspects or rewrites values.\\n\\n## Motivation and goals\\n\\nBlazor applications currently write explicit expressions such as `@Assets[\\\"images/logo.png\\\"]` to resolve fingerprinted static web assets. Common HTML scenarios become repetitive, while automatically treating arbitrary component parameters as asset paths would create silent false positives.\\n\\nThe proposal aims to:\\n\\n- Keep common static asset references concise without adding Razor syntax.\\n- Require explicit component parameter opt-in.\\n- Define a conservative built-in HTML allowlist.\\n- Give component libraries a discoverable opt-in contract.\\n- Preserve existing behavior for nonqualifying values and locations.\\n- Provide a default-on, per-project MSBuild opt-out.\\n\\n## In scope\\n\\n- A public `[AssetPath]` marker for individual string component parameters.\\n- Public `[AcceptsAssetPath(elementName, attributeName)]` metadata for HTML element/attribute pairs.\\n- Razor compile-time expansion of complete static literals beginning exactly with `~/`.\\n- Initial built-in HTML support for `img[src]`, `link[href]`, and `script[src]`.\\n- `RazorEnableAssetPathExpansion`, enabled by default and independently configurable for each application or Razor class library.\\n- Declaration diagnostics for `[AssetPath]` used without `[Parameter]` or on a non-string property.\\n- An audit of built-in Blazor component APIs.\\n\\n## Out of scope\\n\\n- Inferring asset semantics from names such as `Source`, `Src`, `Href`, or `Url`.\\n- Runtime string inspection, runtime registration, middleware, services, or render-tree rewriting.\\n- C# expressions, interpolated values, attribute splatting, CSS, JavaScript, `style`, or `srcset` parsing.\\n- Navigation and submission locations such as `a[href]` and `form[action]`.\\n- Changes to static web asset discovery, fingerprint generation, publication, or lookup fallback.\\n- Adding new string URL parameters to existing built-in components as part of this feature.\\n\\n## Risks / unknowns\\n\\n- Delivery requires coordinated changes in `dotnet/aspnetcore`, `dotnet/roslyn`, and `dotnet/sdk`.\\n- The Razor team must confirm the metadata descriptor mechanism for data consumed by a lowering pass without ordinary tag matching.\\n- The exact Razor language-version gate and package-flow order need agreement.\\n- Custom Razor base classes without a compatible `Assets` member would receive a C# compile error when using the concise syntax.\\n- Supported IDE hosts must be validated for compiler-visible MSBuild property propagation.\\n- API review must confirm names and whether third-party HTML-pair extension remains open.\\n\\n## Examples\\n\\nBuilt-in HTML:\\n\\n```razor\\n\\u003cimg src=\\\"~/images/logo.png\\\" alt=\\\"Company logo\\\" /\\u003e\\n\\u003clink rel=\\\"stylesheet\\\" href=\\\"~/css/site.css\\\" /\\u003e\\n\\u003cscript src=\\\"~/js/app.js\\\"\\u003e\\u003c/script\\u003e\\n```\\n\\nThe Razor compiler generates behavior equivalent to:\\n\\n```razor\\n\\u003cimg src=\\\"@Assets[\\\"images/logo.png\\\"]\\\" alt=\\\"Company logo\\\" /\\u003e\\n\\u003clink rel=\\\"stylesheet\\\" href=\\\"@Assets[\\\"css/site.css\\\"]\\\" /\\u003e\\n\\u003cscript src=\\\"@Assets[\\\"js/app.js\\\"]\\\"\\u003e\\u003c/script\\u003e\\n```\\n\\nComponent opt-in:\\n\\n```csharp\\npublic class Image : ComponentBase\\n{\\n    [Parameter]\\n    [AssetPath]\\n    public string? Source { get; set; }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n```razor\\n\\u003cImage Source=\\\"~/images/logo.png\\\" /\\u003e\\n```\\n\\nThe component receives the same value as:\\n\\n```razor\\n\\u003cImage Source=\\\"@Assets[\\\"images/logo.png\\\"]\\\" /\\u003e\\n```\\n\\nPer-project opt-out:\\n\\n```xml\\n\\u003cPropertyGroup\\u003e\\n  \\u003cRazorEnableAssetPathExpansion\\u003efalse\\u003c/RazorEnableAssetPathExpansion\\u003e\\n\\u003c/PropertyGroup\\u003e\\n```\\n\\nWhen disabled, Razor leaves `~/` literals unchanged in that project's Razor files. The setting cannot transform or undo generated code in a precompiled referenced library. Metadata from referenced component assemblies remains discoverable by an enabled consuming project.\\n\\n# Detailed design\\n\\n## Public API\\n\\n```diff\\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components;\\n\\n+[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Property, AllowMultiple = false, Inherited = true)]\\n+public sealed class AssetPathAttribute : Attribute\\n+{\\n+    public AssetPathAttribute();\\n+}\\n+\\n+[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class, AllowMultiple = true, Inherited = true)]\\n+public sealed class AcceptsAssetPathAttribute : Attribute\\n+{\\n+    public AcceptsAssetPathAttribute(string elementName, string attributeName);\\n+\\n+    public string ElementName { get; }\\n+    public string AttributeName { get; }\\n+}\\n```\\n\\n`[AssetPath]` is valid only on a normal `[Parameter]` whose type is `string` or nullable `string`.\\n\\n## Built-in HTML metadata\\n\\n```csharp\\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web;\\n\\n[AcceptsAssetPath(\\\"img\\\", \\\"src\\\")]\\n[AcceptsAssetPath(\\\"link\\\", \\\"href\\\")]\\n[AcceptsAssetPath(\\\"script\\\", \\\"src\\\")]\\npublic static class AssetPathAttributes\\n{\\n}\\n```\\n\\nRazor discovers public convention classes named `AssetPathAttributes` in referenced assemblies, following the existing `BindAttributes` and `EventHandlers` model. Duplicate pairs are deduplicated.\\n\\nDeferred HTML candidates include `source[src]`, `audio[src]`, `video[src]`, `video[poster]`, `track[src]`, `input[src]`, `iframe[src]`, `embed[src]`, and `object[data]`.\\n\\n## Exact transformation rules\\n\\n- The current project must have `RazorEnableAssetPathExpansion` enabled.\\n- The location must be an opted-in component parameter or allowlisted HTML pair.\\n- The value must be complete static Razor text.\\n- Its first two characters must be exactly `~/`; whitespace is not trimmed.\\n- Razor removes `~/` and emits `Assets[\\\"key\\\"]`.\\n- Dynamic or mixed Razor content is never inspected.\\n- HTML names use ordinal, case-insensitive matching.\\n- Unmapped keys retain existing `ResourceAssetCollection` fallback behavior.\\n\\n## Compiler and SDK architecture\\n\\nASP.NET Core owns the public metadata attributes, built-in declarations, declaration analyzer, public API tests, and rendering coverage. Roslyn owns component property metadata, HTML metadata discovery, intermediate-node lowering, generated-code tests, and compiler integration. The .NET SDK owns the MSBuild default and compiler-visible property flow.\\n\\n`ComponentTagHelperProducer` records `[AssetPath]` as `PropertyMetadata.AcceptsAssetPath`. An asset-path metadata producer converts `[AcceptsAssetPath]` declarations into typed descriptors. A Razor optimization pass runs after component lowering and rewrites only eligible literal nodes into ordinary `Assets[\\\"key\\\"]` expressions.\\n\\n`RazorEnableAssetPathExpansion` flows through a `CompilerVisibleProperty` into `RazorConfiguration.EnableAssetPathExpansion`. Razor registers the producer and lowering pass only when the switch and required Razor language version are enabled. Configuration equality and hashing include the flag so changing it invalidates incremental generated output.\\n\\n## Built-in Blazor component audit\\n\\nNo current public built-in component parameter is both a string and one static web asset path, so the initial component annotation set is empty.\\n\\n| Component or area | Current asset-related API | Decision |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Media.Image` | Required `MediaSource Source`; generates an object URL for `img[src]`. | Defer until a separate static string source API is proposed. |\\n| `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Media.Video` | Required `MediaSource Source`; generates an object URL for `video[src]`; poster is captured metadata. | Defer dedicated string source/poster APIs. |\\n| `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Media.FileDownload` | `MediaSource Source`; `FileName` is an output filename; component controls `href`. | Exclude. |\\n| `NavLink` and `EditForm` | Navigation/submission URLs are captured attributes. | Exclude as non-asset URLs and splatted values. |\\n| Built-in input components | URL-shaped HTML values, where relevant, are captured attributes. | Exclude because splatting is outside the feature. |\\n| `ImportMap` | Structured definition containing multiple mappings. | Exclude from the single-string marker. |\\n| `ResourcePreloader` | Framework-generated resolved preload data and no public path parameter. | Exclude. |\\n| Head components | Fragments or text; nested asset elements compile as ordinary HTML. | Exclude from parameter annotations. |\\n| QuickGrid and authentication components | Generated navigation/query URLs or route/options models. | Exclude as non-asset URLs. |\\n\\nFuture built-in APIs that introduce one string static asset path should apply `[AssetPath]` when defined.\\n\\n## Validation\\n\\n- Generated-code tests for component and HTML expansion.\\n- Compiler tests proving dynamic and unsupported values remain unchanged.\\n- Analyzer tests for invalid marker placement and type.\\n- Rendering tests for mapped and unmapped assets.\\n- End-to-end tests for static and interactive render modes.\\n- MSBuild tests for default-on behavior, per-project opt-out, design-time propagation, referenced-library behavior, and incremental invalidation.\\n- Public API review for both attributes and `AssetPathAttributes`.\\n\\n## Considered alternatives\\n\\n- Name-based or all-string parameter inference: rejected due to false positives.\\n- New Razor syntax: rejected due to parser and language-surface cost.\\n- Hardcoded HTML pairs in Razor: rejected because it couples ASP.NET Core policy to the compiler.\\n- Runtime render-tree rewriting or runtime switch: rejected because this is an authoring-time transformation.\\n- Attribute splatting support: rejected because it loses individual parameter opt-in and static-literal If we use Razor Pages with static assets, the rendered pages will be using the fingerprinted resources and the import map is generated fine.\n\nAdditionally, I've been digging a bit, and I think that the problem is that `MapControllerRoute()` -and other similar methods like `MapDefaultControllerRoute()`- are returning a builder that does not contain the item required by `WithStaticAssets()` to do its magic.\n\nIn fact, we can make it work using reflection: \n\n```cs\n... // Other Program.cs code\n\n// Replace this:\n// app.MapControllerRoute(\n//    name: \"default\",\n//    pattern: .GetProperty(\"Items\", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance);\n\nvar itemsPropertyDictionary = itemsProperty.GetValue(controllerActionEndpointConventionBuilder) as Dictionary\u003cstring, object\u003e;\nitemsPropertyDictionary?.Add(\"__EndpointRouteBuilder\", app);\ncontrollerActionEndpointConventionBuilder.WithStaticAssets();\n// End patch\n```\n\nI hope it can help to pinpoint the Use this before fixating on a particular implementation.\n--\u003e\n\n## Summary\n\n.NET 10 made `.MapStaticAssets()` the only way to serve `blazor.server.js` and `blazor.web.js` even though `blazor.webassembly.js` is served just fine without it. When using `.UseStaticFiles()`, the new `.AddInteractiveServerComponents()` and the old `.MapBlazorHub()` no longer result in those files being served. This is what #64381 reports.\n\n## Motivation and goals\n\nThis removes the unnecessary overhead of being forced to migrate to `.MapStaticAssets()` when migrating to .NET 10. It also solves the significant headache of discovering that this is the solution to an obscure error in the first place. For example, I personally had to do a lot of research to understand how this would impact my custom Webpack pipeline.\n\n## In scope\n\n- #64381\n  - This is the exact motivating issue.\n\n## Out of scope\n\n- #57756\n  - `.UseBlazorFrameworkFiles()` and `.MapBlazorHub()` are wrapped by the newer `.AddInteractiveWebAssemblyComponents()` and `.AddInteractiveServerComponents()` respectively, both of which are designed to play nice with `.MapStaticAssets()`. This could be solved by the methods performing the same check and throwing an exception if static assets are mapped. Not relevant to this though.\n\n## Risks / unknowns\n\nThis restores half-deleted functionality (only the server side) and without clear guidance as to how to adapt without having to search through GitHub issues. I don't believe this is a risk or blocker for future features.\n\n## Examples\n\nIn the following examples, `.MapStaticAssets()` is NOT called, and it's assumed that `.UseRouting()` is called before `.UseStaticFiles()` so that the static files middleware is endpoint-aware. The following no longer works in .NET 10:\n\n```cs\napp.UseStaticFiles();\napp.MapRazorComponents().AddInteractiveServerComponents();\n```\n\n```cs\napp.UseStaticFiles();\napp.MapBlazorHub();\n```\n\nBut these still do:\n\n```cs\napp.UseStaticFiles();\napp.MapRazorComponents().AddInteractiveWebAssemblyComponents();\n```\n\n```cs\napp.UseStaticFiles();\napp.UseBlazorFrameworkFiles();\n```\n\nBoth should work.\n\n# Research\n\nThis issue appears to be a mistake, not an intentional change. Here's the timeline I discovered:\n\n1. The static asset guard is introduced to only the wasm endpoints. It is never added to the server endpoints. See: #55558\n2. The static asset guard is changed from `if (wasmWithOptions is { EndpointOptions.ConventionsApplied: true })` to `if (applicationBuilder.Properties[ResourceCollectionKey] is ResourceAssetCollection assetMap)`. See: #56045\n3. At some point, the unified endpoint `blazor.web.js` is added into the mix. See: #47605\n4. #58721 implements the switch to serving `blazor.*.js` files as static assets. In the same batch of changes, however, the server endpoints are just dropped entirely. Presumably this made sense without the context of this papertrail.\n\n# Detailed design\n\nGiven the evidence, I believe the correct (and very simple) fix is to re-add the server and unified endpoints (`blazor.server.js` and `blazor.web.js`), but under the same guard as the wasm endpoints. This was likely the correct course of action to begin with when looking at the big picture.\n\n## Key decisions\n\n- Since the old versions of the endpoints read from embedded resources, the new versions will instead mimic how the wasm endpoints are read from static files.\n- The old versions returned the map files for the `blazor.*.js` files guarded by `#if DEBUG` for internal testing purposes. Given that they were removed and probably are configured to exist as static assets for internal testing, these will not be added back.\n- The wasm endpoints have very elaborate static files options, whereas the server and unified endpoints had very basic ones. My research showed that this was not the unified and server endpoints falling behind; rather, the requirements for them were considerably more simple since they're singular JS files. This will be preserved.\n- There are slight inconsistencies between the endpoint configuration for `blazor.server.js` and `blazor.web.js`. These will be preserved.\n- `blazor.web.js` received a feature improvement that makes it configurable e.g. with `[AllowAnonymous]`, but the same improvement was not made to `blazor.server.js` even though it existed at the time. This will be preserved. See: #57086\n\n## Open questions\n\n- I am not sure what the right way to get whether static assets are active/present to the endpoint builder helpers. I have left these as TODOs. I am a bit suspicious of the current pattern that almost seems to hijack the app builder properties in order to communicate across route config calls, and even that comes after scraping the result of static assets config off an arbitrary endpoint.\n\n## Draft implementation\n\nThis is a relatively simple change to a system that's a bit of a maze, so I figured a simple draft PR would help get the ideas across. The PR is broken up into digestible commits. See: #66060\n\n\u003c!--\nIt's often best not to fill this out until you get basic consensus about the above. solution: a WPF project that uses WebView2, a Web project that has Controllers for API calls, and a JavaScript project (esproj) that uses Vue.js. The WPF project (Microsoft.NET.Sdk) references the Web project (Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web), and the Web project references the JS project (Microsoft.VisualStudio.JavaScript.Sdk).\r\n\r\nThe way things worked until recently was that we would publish the WPF project, and the published output would include a wwwroot folder with the contents of the \"dist\" folder from running \"npm run build\". We'd then run our executable in the publish folder and it would be able to access the wwwroot and correctly render the site in our hybrid desktop app.\r\n\r\nWe noticed an issue in our CI pipeline with building our JS project on a Linux build server. The build server complained it needed .NET Framework installed and that was why it couldn't build the JS project. The esproj SDK version for the JS project is 0.5.94-alpha. I can't remember if it was on a whim or a recommendation I found online, but I upgraded the JS SDK version to a slightly newer version of 0.5.128-alpha and the CI pipeline build worked!\r\n\r\nFor reference, the code change in the esproj file was simply going from:\r\n```﻿\u003cProject Sdk=\"Microsoft.VisualStudio.JavaScript.Sdk/0.5.94-alpha\"\u003e```\r\nto\r\n```﻿\u003cProject Sdk=\"Microsoft.VisualStudio.JavaScript.Sdk/0.5.128-alpha\"\u003e```\r\n\r\nHowever, when we published the project, the \"wwwroot\" folder was no longing being added to the publish output.\r\n\r\nI decided to make a new project in Visual Studio using the \"Vue and ASP.NET Core\" project template to see if the wwwroot folder was created when publishing the code from the project template. It did create wwwroot with the project template code. So, I started wondering what the difference was between my code and the template's. For starters, I found the esproj JS SDK version was higher in the project template (it used 1.0.784122). I tried the same exact version from the template and my project still did not produce a wwwroot folder when publishing.\r\n\r\nAfter trying many things, I finally found a solution that worked. It required 3 changes. \r\n\r\n1. I changed my WPF project to use the Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web SDK. So the change in my csproj file was\r\n```\u003cProject Sdk=\"Microsoft.NET.Sdk\"\u003e```\r\nto\r\n```\u003cProject Sdk=\"Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web\"\u003e```\r\n2. I mentioned above that the project hierarchy we have is: WPF project references the Web project, and the Web project references the JS project. I had to make my WPF project directly reference the JS project\r\n3. Updates to my pubxml file for Web publishing vs Desktop publishing (e.g. using the \"PublishUrl\" property rather than the \"PublishDir\" property)\r\n\r\nAfter those 3 changes, I was now getting a wwwroot folder in my published output.\r\n\r\nThis would've been a working solution; however, a new problem arose. Now, the \"EnvironmentName\" property in my pubxml file was not overwriting the value of the \"EnvironmentName\" property in my WPF csproj file while publishing. That impacted a custom MsBuild target I have for post-publishing (including environment name in a zip file of our published output), and it also impacted how the environment was set during runtime.\r\n\r\n### Expected Behavior\r\n\r\nPublishing a non-Web SDK project that references a newer JS esproj project produces a wwwroot folder in the published output.\r\n\r\n### Steps To Reproduce\r\n\r\nFirst clone the repo on a Windows machine. \r\n\r\nhttps://github.com/dustinrowland12/DotNetHybridApp\r\n\r\nA few notes about the repo:\r\n- The repo is setup with the old JS SDK to first demonstrate the expected working behavior.\r\n- The repo is setup with the same project structure as described in the bug section of this ticket (WPF project with WebView2 referencing Web project referencing JS project with Vue.js)\r\n- I started with the \"Vue and ASP.NET Core\" project template. Describe the bug\r\n\r\nThe Web SDK does not normally publish `*.cshtml` files when using `dotnet publish` (because they're precompiled into the web site assembly and aren't needed). These files are published from referenced projects if `$(NoBuild)` is `true` e.g. using `dotnet publish --no-build`. These files increase deployment payloads and can confuse tests.\r\n\r\n### To Reproduce\r\n\u003c!--\r\nWe ❤ code! Point us to a minimalistic repro project hosted in a GitHub repo, Gist snippet, or other means to see the isolated behavior.\r\n\r\nWe may close this issue if:\r\n- the repro project you share with us is complex. We can't investigate custom projects, so don't point us to such, please.\r\n- if we will not be able to repro the behavior you're reporting\r\n--\u003e\r\n\r\n1. In a clone of the dotnet/aspnetcore repo, run `eng\\build.cmd -noBuildManaged -noBuildNative`\r\n2. `dotnet build src\\Mvc\\test\\WebSites\\RazorPagesWebSite\\`\r\n3. `dotnet publish --no-build src\\Mvc\\test\\WebSites\\RazorPagesWebSite\\`\r\n4. Observe the artifacts\\bin\\RazorPagesWebSite\\Debug\\net7.0\\publish\\Pages\\ClassLibraryPages folder as well as the `*.cshtml` files within it\r\n5. Reset using `rm -Recurse artifacts\\bin\\RazorPagesWebSite\\` and `rm -Recurse artifacts\\obj\\RazorPagesWebSite\\`\r\n6. `dotnet build src\\Mvc\\test\\WebSites\\RazorPagesWebSite\\`\r\n7. `dotnet publish src\\Mvc\\test\\WebSites\\RazorPagesWebSite\\`\r\n8. Observe the **lack of** an artifacts\\bin\\RazorPagesWebSite\\Debug\\net7.0\\publish\\Pages folder\r\n\r\n### More detail\r\n\r\nUsing `/p:BuildProjectReferences=false` instead of `--no-build` in step 3 results in the same over-publication.\r\n\r\nThe ClassLibraryPages folder comes from the referenced src\\Mvc\\test\\WebSites\\RazorPagesClassLibrary\\ project. Note the many `*.cshtml` files from the RazorPagesWebSite project are **not** published in either (3) or (7).\r\n\r\nMoving up a project dependency level and doing the same with the src\\Mvc\\test\\Mvc.FunctionalTests\\ project is worse because src\\Mvc\\test\\WebSites\\RazorPagesWebSite\\ contains a lot of `*.cshtml` files and other referenced projects add to that; all are copied into artifacts\\bin\\Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.FunctionalTests\\Debug\\net7.0\\publish\\Pages and \u0026hellip;\\Views. This breaks the functional tests because a few test sites use `\u003cRazorCompileOnPublish\u003efalse\u003c/RazorCompileOnPublish\u003e` and pick up incorrect / unexpected files.\r\n\r\n#### Binary logging\r\n\r\nThe `AssignTargetPaths` target in the RazorPagesClassLibrary project adds`@(ContentWithTargetPath)` for `Pages\\ClassLibraryPages\\*.cshtml` in all cases. Summary\n\nAdd an opt-out Razor compile-time transformation that rewrites literal `~/...` static asset paths into equivalent `Assets[\"...\"]` expressions for explicitly opted-in component parameters and a conservative set of HTML attributes.\n\nRuntime assemblies only provide metadata attributes and built-in declarations for Razor to discover. No runtime code inspects or rewrites values.\n\n## Motivation and goals\n\nBlazor applications currently write explicit expressions such as `@Assets[\"images/logo.png\"]` to resolve fingerprinted static web assets. Common HTML scenarios become repetitive, while automatically treating arbitrary component parameters as asset paths would create silent false positives.\n\nThe proposal aims to:\n\n- Keep common static asset references concise without adding Razor syntax.\n- Require explicit component parameter opt-in.\n- Define a conservative built-in HTML allowlist.\n- Give component libraries a discoverable opt-in contract.\n- Preserve existing behavior for nonqualifying values and locations.\n- Provide a default-on, per-project MSBuild opt-out.\n\n## In scope\n\n- A public `[AssetPath]` marker for individual string component parameters.\n- Public `[AcceptsAssetPath(elementName, attributeName)]` metadata for HTML element/attribute pairs.\n- Razor compile-time expansion of complete static literals beginning exactly with `~/`.\n- Initial built-in HTML support for `img[src]`, `link[href]`, and `script[src]`.\n- `RazorEnableAssetPathExpansion`, enabled by default and independently configurable for each application or Razor class library.\n- Declaration diagnostics for `[AssetPath]` used without `[Parameter]` or on a non-string property.\n- An audit of built-in Blazor component APIs.\n\n## Out of scope\n\n- Inferring asset semantics from names such as `Source`, `Src`, `Href`, or `Url`.\n- Runtime string inspection, runtime registration, middleware, services, or render-tree rewriting.\n- C# expressions, interpolated values, attribute splatting, CSS, JavaScript, `style`, or `srcset` parsing.\n- Navigation and submission locations such as `a[href]` and `form[action]`.\n- Changes to static web asset discovery, fingerprint generation, publication, or lookup fallback.\n- Adding new string URL parameters to existing built-in components as part of this feature.\n\n## Risks / unknowns\n\n- Delivery requires coordinated changes in `dotnet/aspnetcore`, `dotnet/roslyn`, and `dotnet/sdk`.\n- The Razor team must confirm the metadata descriptor mechanism for data consumed by a lowering pass without ordinary tag matching.\n- The exact Razor language-version gate and package-flow order need agreement.\n- Custom Razor base classes without a compatible `Assets` member would receive a C# compile error when using the concise syntax.\n- Supported IDE hosts must be validated for compiler-visible MSBuild property propagation.\n- API review must confirm names and whether third-party HTML-pair extension remains open.\n\n## Examples\n\nBuilt-in HTML:\n\n```razor\n\u003cimg src=\"~/images/logo.png\" alt=\"Company logo\" /\u003e\n\u003clink rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"~/css/site.css\" /\u003e\n\u003cscript src=\"~/js/app.js\"\u003e\u003c/script\u003e\n```\n\nThe Razor compiler generates behavior equivalent to:\n\n```razor\n\u003cimg src=\"@Assets[\"images/logo.png\"]\" alt=\"Company logo\" /\u003e\n\u003clink rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"@Assets[\"css/site.css\"]\" /\u003e\n\u003cscript src=\"@Assets[\"js/app.js\"]\"\u003e\u003c/script\u003e\n```\n\nComponent opt-in:\n\n```csharp\npublic class Image : ComponentBase\n{\n    [Parameter]\n    [AssetPath]\n    public string? Source { get; set; }\n}\n```\n\n```razor\n\u003cImage Source=\"~/images/logo.png\" /\u003e\n```\n\nThe component receives the same value as:\n\n```razor\n\u003cImage Source=\"@Assets[\"images/logo.png\"]\" /\u003e\n```\n\nPer-project opt-out:\n\n```xml\n\u003cPropertyGroup\u003e\n  \u003cRazorEnableAssetPathExpansion\u003efalse\u003c/RazorEnableAssetPathExpansion\u003e\n\u003c/PropertyGroup\u003e\n```\n\nWhen disabled, Razor leaves `~/` literals unchanged in that project's Razor files. The setting cannot transform or undo generated code in a precompiled referenced library. Metadata from referenced component assemblies remains discoverable by an enabled consuming project.\n\n# Detailed design\n\n## Public API\n\n```diff\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components;\n\n+[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Property, AllowMultiple = false, Inherited = true)]\n+public sealed class AssetPathAttribute : Attribute\n+{\n+    public AssetPathAttribute();\n+}\n+\n+[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class, AllowMultiple = true, Inherited = true)]\n+public sealed class AcceptsAssetPathAttribute : Attribute\n+{\n+    public AcceptsAssetPathAttribute(string elementName, string attributeName);\n+\n+    public string ElementName { get; }\n+    public string AttributeName { get; }\n+}\n```\n\n`[AssetPath]` is valid only on a normal `[Parameter]` whose type is `string` or nullable `string`.\n\n## Built-in HTML metadata\n\n```csharp\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web;\n\n[AcceptsAssetPath(\"img\", \"src\")]\n[AcceptsAssetPath(\"link\", \"href\")]\n[AcceptsAssetPath(\"script\", \"src\")]\npublic static class AssetPathAttributes\n{\n}\n```\n\nRazor discovers public convention classes named `AssetPathAttributes` in referenced assemblies, following the existing `BindAttributes` and `EventHandlers` model. Duplicate pairs are deduplicated.\n\nDeferred HTML candidates include `source[src]`, `audio[src]`, `video[src]`, `video[poster]`, `track[src]`, `input[src]`, `iframe[src]`, `embed[src]`, and `object[data]`.\n\n## Exact transformation rules\n\n- The current project must have `RazorEnableAssetPathExpansion` enabled.\n- The location must be an opted-in component parameter or allowlisted HTML pair.\n- The value must be complete static Razor text.\n- Its first two characters must be exactly `~/`; whitespace is not trimmed.\n- Razor removes `~/` and emits `Assets[\"key\"]`.\n- Dynamic or mixed Razor content is never inspected.\n- HTML names use ordinal, case-insensitive matching.\n- Unmapped keys retain existing `ResourceAssetCollection` fallback behavior.\n\n## Compiler and SDK architecture\n\nASP.NET Core owns the public metadata attributes, built-in declarations, declaration analyzer, public API tests, and rendering coverage. Roslyn owns component property metadata, HTML metadata discovery, intermediate-node lowering, generated-code tests, and compiler integration. The .NET SDK owns the MSBuild default and compiler-visible property flow.\n\n`ComponentTagHelperProducer` records `[AssetPath]` as `PropertyMetadata.AcceptsAssetPath`. An asset-path metadata producer converts `[AcceptsAssetPath]` declarations into typed descriptors. A Razor optimization pass runs after component lowering and rewrites only eligible literal nodes into ordinary `Assets[\"key\"]` expressions.\n\n`RazorEnableAssetPathExpansion` flows through a `CompilerVisibleProperty` into `RazorConfiguration.EnableAssetPathExpansion`. Razor registers the producer and lowering pass only when the switch and required Razor language version are enabled. Configuration equality and hashing include the flag so changing it invalidates incremental generated output.\n\n## Built-in Blazor component audit\n\nNo current public built-in component parameter is both a string and one static web asset path, so the initial component annotation set is empty.\n\n| Component or area | Current asset-related API | Decision |\n|---|---|---|\n| `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Media.Image` | Required `MediaSource Source`; generates an object URL for `img[src]`. | Defer until a separate static string source API is proposed. |\n| `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Media.Video` | Required `MediaSource Source`; generates an object URL for `video[src]`; poster is captured metadata. | Defer dedicated string source/poster APIs. |\n| `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Media.FileDownload` | `MediaSource Source`; `FileName` is an output filename; component controls `href`. | Exclude. |\n| `NavLink` and `EditForm` | Navigation/submission URLs are captured attributes. | Exclude as non-asset URLs and splatted values. |\n| Built-in input components | URL-shaped HTML values, where relevant, are captured attributes. | Exclude because splatting is outside the feature. |\n| `ImportMap` | Structured definition containing multiple mappings. | Exclude from the single-string marker. |\n| `ResourcePreloader` | Framework-generated resolved preload data and no public path parameter. | Exclude. |\n| Head components | Fragments or text; nested asset elements compile as ordinary HTML. | Exclude from parameter annotations. |\n| QuickGrid and authentication components | Generated navigation/query URLs or route/options models. | Exclude as non-asset URLs. |\n\nFuture built-in APIs that introduce one string static asset path should apply `[AssetPath]` when defined.\n\n## Validation\n\n- Generated-code tests for component and HTML expansion.\n- Compiler tests proving dynamic and unsupported values remain unchanged.\n- Analyzer tests for invalid marker placement and type.\n- Rendering tests for mapped and unmapped assets.\n- End-to-end tests for static and interactive render modes.\n- MSBuild tests for default-on behavior, per-project opt-out, design-time propagation, referenced-library behavior, and incremental invalidation.\n- Public API review for both attributes and `AssetPathAttributes`.\n\n## Considered alternatives\n\n- Name-based or all-string parameter inference: rejected due to false positives.\n- New Razor syntax: rejected due to parser and language-surface cost.\n- Hardcoded HTML pairs in Razor: rejected because it couples ASP.NET Core policy to the compiler.\n- Runtime render-tree rewriting or runtime switch: rejected because this is an authoring-time transformation.\n- contact:** @javiercn\\n\\n## Scenario\\n\\n**This scenario validates that a fix works.** A native app hosting Blazor is closed, backgrounded and navigated around far more abruptly than a web page, and its components are often in the middle of talking to JavaScript when that happens. Disposing an `IJSObjectReference` after the WebView had gone threw `JSDisconnectedException`, which showed up as hangs on teardown and alarming errors in the debug output. Navigation and disposal now mark the JS runtime disconnected before components are disposed, and that exception is caught and discarded.\\n\\nThis validates that a Hybrid app tears down cleanly.\\n\\n## Minimum build\\n\\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\\n\\n## Configurations to cover\\n\\n* Blazor Web App\\n  * [ ] Static SSR\\n  * [ ] Interactive Server\\n  * [ ] Interactive WebAssembly\\n  * [ ] Interactive Auto\\n* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly\\n* [x] Hybrid (MAUI)\\n\\n## Also exercise\\n\\n* [ ] Published output\\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\\n* [ ] Hot Reload\\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\\n* [ ] Container\\n\\n## Setup\\n\\nYou need the workloads for building a native app for at least one platform, and a device or emulator. Covering more than one platform is worthwhile, since the embedded browser differs between them.\\n\\n## What to build\\n\\nA native app hosting Blazor, with pages that are busy in ways that make teardown awkward. Include a page that keeps a JavaScript module loaded and calls into it repeatedly, one that starts a slow JavaScript call and does not wait for it, one with a timer that keeps firing, and one that has registered .NET methods for JavaScript to call back into. Give the components proper cleanup so you can tell whether it runs. Add a native page alongside the Blazor content so you can move between the two kinds of screen, and log to the debug output when each component is cleaned up.\\n\\n## Things to try\\n\\n* Navigating away from each busy page while it is mid-flight.\\n* Moving from a Blazor screen to a native screen and back, repeatedly.\\n* Closing the app while a page is in the middle of a JavaScript call.\\n* Backgrounding the app and returning to it, and backgrounding it and then closing it.\\n* Using the operating system's back gesture or button rather than in-app navigation.\\n* Rotating the device while a page is busy.\\n* Repeating the cycle many times in one session and watching memory.\\n* Watching the debug output throughout for exceptions and warnings.\\n\\n## Expected behavior\\n\\nTeardown completes promptly however busy the page was, and calls that were already in flight go quietly.\\n\\n### Must hold\\n\\n* Leaving each busy page runs its cleanup and does not hang.\\n* Closing the app while a JavaScript call is in flight terminates promptly rather than waiting on work that will never finish.\\n* No exception from calls that were in flight appears in the debug output. In particular, disposing a JavaScript object reference after the connection is gone must not surface a `JSDisconnectedException`.\\n* Repeated moves between Blazor and native screens leave memory stable across the session.\\n* Returning from the background finds the app in a working state.\\n\\n### Expected differences between configurations\\n\\n* The embedded browser differs between platforms, so cover more than one if you can. A teardown that is clean on one platform and not on another is a finding.\\n\\n## Documentation to use\\n\\n* [ASP.NET Core Blazor Hybrid](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/hybrid/?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\\n* [Component disposal](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/components/component-disposal?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\\n\\n## What to report\\n\\nReport results using the format described in the [validation testing manual](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/68479). is best for the current user's browser:\\r\\n\\r\\n * **On the browser's main JS thread**, which is necessary for older browsers that don't support WebWorker. The .NET/JS interop can continue using shared memory if we find it's necessary to have good perf on those older browsers (and thread safety is not difficult because it's all synchronous).\\r\\n * **In a web worker (background thread) on more up-to-date browsers**. The .NET/JS interop will need to work by serializing any data that is being transferred rather than passing pointers [1].\\r\\n\\r\\nThis will be advantageous because then, even if your .NET code does something that locks up the CPU (such as a GC cycle), the UI will remain perfectly smooth (e.g., during animations or scrolling, or while the user is typing quickly into a textbox).\\r\\n\\r\\nThe existing UI update mechanism is designed around transferring batches of minimal diffs from .NET to JS, so it shouldn't be hugely difficult to have it express those diffs as serialized data rather than pointers into the WASM memory space. We'll have to be careful around things like event handling to ensure that the asynchrony can't result in inconsistency of behaviour versus the synchronous single-threaded model. For example, we will need to force all event delivery to be async as far as the JS side is concerned, even in the non-worker-thread case.\\r\\n\\r\\n*[1] Strictly speaking, we could also do it with shared memory on even newer browsers that support SharedArrayBuffer. But if we can get satisfactory perf without this, it would be better to serialize because it would mean fewer combinations of browser scenarios, and saves us having to deal with potentially complex .NET trimmer statically analyzes your project and removes any unused code. In Blazor we use the .NET trimmer to significantly reduce the publish size of Blazor WebAssembly apps. However, we don't currently use the .NET trimmer to its fullest potential. We currently configure the trimmer in a partial mode, which only trims assemblies that are explicitly marked as trimmable. This typically means that the app assembly itself and many dependencies are not trimmed. This is a conservative setting that optimizes for maintaining functionality over reducing app size. \\r\\n\\r\\nThe default trim mode for the .NET trimmer is to trim everything. This is the mode used by the .NET Native AOT workloads.Analyzers provide warnings if there are code paths in the app that are not safe to trim. Given how sensitive web apps are to download size and load time, it seems like doing full trimming should be the goal for Blazor.\\r\\n\\r\\nEnabling support for full trimming also is a potential solution to enabling a [single project model for Blazor Web Apps](#49079) that target both server and browser. When you multitarget a project, everything in the project is built for both targets unless you indicated otherwise. This is problematic for browser scenarios because you may potentially bring in dependencies, components, and code into the browser targeted build that are only needed on the server. However, if we could enable full trimming *and* indicate to the trimmer which components are setup to render on WebAssembly, then the browser build could be aggressively trimmed to remove any unwanted code and dependencies.\\r\\n\\r\\nEnabling support for full .NET trimming typically means removing any dynamic code path that are based on reflection. We would need to make Blazor apps trimmer friendly by removing this code using techniques like source generators. For example, in Blazor we use reflection as part of the component discovery process and in the render tree builder code generated by the Razor compiler. We're already working on enabling [component discovery through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/48767). We also have on our backlog to [handle component parameters through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/29550). There may be other related work items as well.\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is also ecosystem impact of enabling full trimming by default. Many .NET libraries are not setup for trimming and would potentially need to be updated. It will take some time to work through these issues with the Blazor community. Certain features also simply wouldn't work with full trimming. For example, dynamically loading dependencies at runtime that are not known statically. For backwards compatibility, app developers can configure the trimmer to not trim assemblies that are not yet trimmer friendly. We'd need to understand better all the cases that get impacted by full trimming and ensure we provide a reasonable user experience for addressing On investigation the problem is that C# has added a new syntax that doesn't work in Razor.**\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Razor compiler allows arbitrary C# code within `@{ ... }` blocks. Unfortunately this means it allows the use of local functions in a way that confuses the parsing logic, causing it to use the wrong `__builder` instance. Example:\\r\\n\\r\\n```razor\\r\\n\\u003cFluentTreeView\\u003e\\r\\n@{\\r\\n    RenderTree(0, 3);\\r\\n\\r\\n    void RenderTree(int depth, int maxDepth)\\r\\n    {\\r\\n        if (depth \\u003e= maxDepth)\\r\\n        {\\r\\n            return;\\r\\n        }\\r\\n\\r\\n        \\u003cFluentTreeItem Text=\\\"item\\\"\\u003e\\r\\n            @{ RenderTree(depth + 1, maxDepth); }\\r\\n        \\u003c/FluentTreeItem\\u003e\\r\\n    }\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\u003c/FluentTreeView\\u003e\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nHere, the child content of `FluentTreeItem` should be compiled as a `RenderFragment` that acts on whatever `RenderTreeBuilder` is passed in. But because of C# scoping rules, the `RenderFragment` actually acts on the `__builder` captured from its parent context, so it is simply corrupting the output instead of doing something useful.\\r\\n\\r\\nPossible solutions:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. We could ask for the Razor compiler block the use of local functions inside `@{ ... }` specifically. However that's probably impractical because Razor doesn't parse the contents of `@{ ... }`.\\r\\n   * Perhaps it is achievable as an analyzer that acts on the code *after* the Razor compiler has generated it.\\r\\n2. We could do something in the runtime to detect more generally any cases where the wrong `RenderTreeBuilder` is invoked. For example if the runtime set an \\\"rendering in progress\\\" flag on it before it starts rendering and synchronously unsets that flag at the end of rendering, then it would have caught this case because child components are rendered afterwards (not recursively), so when the child is rendered it would see it's trying to write to a builder that does not have the \\\"rendering in progress\\\" flag set.\\r\\n   * Drawback: how do we even check if this flag is set? We would **not** check it as part of each rendering instruction. There's plenty of evidence that rendering perf is sensitive to that kind of thing (and we can't just check it in development either).\\r\\n   * Possible solution: instead of just setting a flag, actually null out the referencing to the underlying buffer (storing it in some other field to be swapped back later). Then if anyone tries to write to the builder while it's not marked as rendering-in-progress, they will get a `NullReferenceException` instead of corrupt output. Is there an existing issue for this?\\n\\n- [x] I have searched the existing issues\\n\\n### Describe the bug\\n\\nWhen attempting to call `DotNet.invokeMethodAsync` from a JavaScript file backing a custom Web Component during its initialization (for example, inside `connectedCallback`), the following error is thrown:\\n\\n\\u003e Error: Assertion failed - heap is currently locked\\n\\u003eat mr (blazor.web.js:1:158963)\\n\\u003eat Object.beginInvokeDotNetFromJS\\n\\nThis happens in a Blazor WebAssembly project.The same approach works fine in a .NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid app.\\n\\nI'm aware that calling .NET from JS during component initialization isn't considered a good practice, but invoking .NET methods would help a gradual migration of a legacy web app to Blazor and MAUI. The goal is to integrate Blazor as a backend facade while preserving the existing UI for now, enabling the team to write new code in Blazor moving forward.\\nThe documentation does not appear to impose any restriction that prevents from using this to handle JS calls:  [Link to docs.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/blazor/javascript-interoperability/call-dotnet-from-javascript?view=aspnetcore-9.0#invoke-a-static-net-method)\\n\\n## Minimal repro repo\\n[https://github.com/alexuaua/BlazorDotNetInteropDemo](https://github.com/alexuaua/BlazorDotNetInteropDemo)\\n\\n## Steps to reproduce\\n1. Clone the repo.\\n2. Run the project and switch to the Counter page.\\n3. Open the browser console.\\n4. Observe the `heap is currently locked` error (only) during initialization  of the web component.\\n\\n## Expected behaviour\\nThe JS-to-.NET interop call should succeed (as it does in MAUI Blazor), or there should be a documented workaround for such use cases. Alternatively, the documentation should clearly explain the restrictions on using DotNet.invokeMethodAsync in Blazor WebAssembly apps.\\n\\n## Actual behaviour\\nThe interop call fails due to what appears to be a race condition.\\n\\nDeferring the call using `setTimeout` (i.e. placing the call later in the stack) resolves the issue, this workaround is even shown in community resources like [Blazor University](https://blazor-university.com/javascript-interop/calling-dotnet-from-javascript/calling-static-dotnet-methods/). \\n\\nThat said, it would be **very helpful if**:\\n- The official documentation explicitly described this race condition and recommended patterns for `DotNet.invokeMethodAsync` in component scenarios.\\n- Blazor could provide a way to queue interop calls that are attempted during initialization - would be helpful for migration projects where modifying component logic is non-trivial.\\nUnless I’m missing something, the tasks performed in the demo do not require synchronous execution. Blazor WebAssembly’s rendering engine is based on its own component lifecycle and does not track or wait for hydration of external DOM elements, such as those created by Web Components.\\n\\nThis issue blocks a real-world migration scenario where we cannot immediately rewrite all UI in Blazor. Any workaround or clarification on supported interop timing would be appreciated.\\n\\n## Related issues\\n- [dotnet/aspnetcore#26809](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/26809) also a race Summary\\r\\nMark the `IApplicationBuilder.UseWebAssemblyDebugging()` extension (in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server`) as obsolete and stop emitting it from our project templates. Modern IDEs (Visual Studio, VS Code) launch the debug proxy directly. This does mean that the legacy in-browser (Ctrl+Alt+D) will no longer be supported.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Background\\r\\n- `UseWebAssemblyDebugging()` is defined in `src/Components/WebAssembly/Server/src/WebAssemblyNetDebugProxyAppBuilderExtensions.cs`. It maps `/_framework/debug` and uses `DebugProxyLauncher` to start the browser debug proxy (`BlazorDebugProxy/BrowserDebugHost.dll`) for the legacy Chromium/Firefox in-browser experience.\\r\\n- Related configuration that only exists to support this path:\\r\\n  - The `inspectUri` value in `launchSettings.json` (`.../_framework/debug/ws-proxy?browser={browserInspectUri}`). This is present in test assets but **not** in the shipping templates.\\r\\n  - `NO_PROXY` handling and the `/_framework/debug` endpoint, both internal to the middleware/launcher.\\r\\n- The IDE-driven debugger launches the debug proxy directly and does not depend on this middleware.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Customer impact\\r\\nUsage of the legacy in-browser debugging path appears low. The strongest signal is #61559 (Apr 2025), where browser debugging was broken out of the box on recent Chromium versions for roughly a month; it drew only 11 distinct commenters and no upvotes, and overall issue volume for this path is very small. We may still receive some complaints from users who rely on browser-only debugging (e.g. without Visual Studio, or in Firefox), so we should be sensitive to that in messaging.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Proposed changes\\r\\n1. **Obsolete the API** — Add `[Obsolete]` to `WebAssemblyNetDebugProxyAppBuilderExtensions.UseWebAssemblyDebugging`, using the next diagnostic ID (`ASPDEPR011`) and a new `AspNetCoreDeprecate011Url` entry in `src/Shared/Obsoletions.cs`. Update the public API baseline files (`PublicAPI.Shipped.txt` / `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt`).\\r\\n\\r\\n   Obsoletion message:\\r\\n   \\u003e `\\\"UseWebAssemblyDebugging is obsolete and should be removed along with any inspectUri configurations. Blazor WebAssembly debugging is now launched directly by Visual Studio and Visual Studio Code.\\\"`\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Remove from the Blazor Web App template** — Remove `app.UseWebAssemblyDebugging();` (guarded by `#if (UseWebAssembly)`) from:\\r\\n   - `src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/BlazorWebCSharp.1/Program.cs`\\r\\n   - `src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/BlazorWebCSharp.1/Program.Main.cs`\\r\\n\\r\\n   Collapse the now-redundant `#if (UseWebAssembly || IndividualLocalAuth)` / `#if (UseWebAssembly)` conditionals accordingly, and update template baseline/snapshot tests.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Standalone Blazor WebAssembly template** — Verified no change needed: `ComponentsWebAssembly-CSharp` is client-only and does not reference `UseWebAssemblyDebugging` or `inspectUri`.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Resolve the internal caller** — `src/Components/WebAssembly/DevServer/src/Server/Startup.cs` calls `UseWebAssemblyDebugging()`. Suppress the new obsoletion warning there (with a justifying comment) so the repo continues to build.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Related work\\r\\n- Companion issue: Deprecate the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` package — contact:** @javiercn\n\n## Scenario\n\n**This scenario validates that a fix works.** A native app hosting Blazor is closed, backgrounded and navigated around far more abruptly than a web page, and its components are often in the middle of talking to JavaScript when that happens. Disposing an `IJSObjectReference` after the WebView had gone threw `JSDisconnectedException`, which showed up as hangs on teardown and alarming errors in the debug output. Navigation and disposal now mark the JS runtime disconnected before components are disposed, and that exception is caught and discarded.\n\nThis validates that a Hybrid app tears down cleanly.\n\n## Minimum build\n\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\n\n## Configurations to cover\n\n* Blazor Web App\n  * [ ] Static SSR\n  * [ ] Interactive Server\n  * [ ] Interactive WebAssembly\n  * [ ] Interactive Auto\n* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly\n* [x] Hybrid (MAUI)\n\n## Also exercise\n\n* [ ] Published output\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\n* [ ] Hot Reload\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\n* [ ] Container\n\n## Setup\n\nYou need the workloads for building a native app for at least one platform, and a device or emulator. Covering more than one platform is worthwhile, since the embedded browser differs between them.\n\n## What to build\n\nA native app hosting Blazor, with pages that are busy in ways that make teardown awkward. Include a page that keeps a JavaScript module loaded and calls into it repeatedly, one that starts a slow JavaScript call and does not wait for it, one with a timer that keeps firing, and one that has registered .NET methods for JavaScript to call back into. Give the components proper cleanup so you can tell whether it runs. Add a native page alongside the Blazor content so you can move between the two kinds of screen, and log to the debug output when each component is cleaned up.\n\n## Things to try\n\n* Navigating away from each busy page while it is mid-flight.\n* Moving from a Blazor screen to a native screen and back, repeatedly.\n* Closing the app while a page is in the middle of a JavaScript call.\n* Backgrounding the app and returning to it, and backgrounding it and then closing it.\n* Using the operating system's back gesture or button rather than in-app navigation.\n* Rotating the device while a page is busy.\n* Repeating the cycle many times in one session and watching memory.\n* Watching the debug output throughout for exceptions and warnings.\n\n## Expected behavior\n\nTeardown completes promptly however busy the page was, and calls that were already in flight go quietly.\n\n### Must hold\n\n* Leaving each busy page runs its cleanup and does not hang.\n* Closing the app while a JavaScript call is in flight terminates promptly rather than waiting on work that will never finish.\n* No exception from calls that were in flight appears in the debug output. In particular, disposing a JavaScript object reference after the connection is gone must not surface a `JSDisconnectedException`.\n* Repeated moves between Blazor and native screens leave memory stable across the session.\n* Returning from the background finds the app in a working state.\n\n### Expected differences between configurations\n\n* The embedded browser differs between platforms, so cover more than one if you can. A teardown that is clean on one platform and not on another is a finding.\n\n## Documentation to use\n\n* [ASP.NET Core Blazor Hybrid](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/hybrid/?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\n* [Component disposal](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/components/component-disposal?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\n\n## What to report\n\nReport results using the format described in the [validation testing manual](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/68479). will be a while before we get to this, but various parts of the architecture are already designed with this in mind.\r\n\r\nWe should support running Blazor in two modes, auto-selecting which one is best for the current user's browser:\r\n\r\n * **On the browser's main JS thread**, which is necessary for older browsers that don't support WebWorker. The .NET/JS interop can continue using shared memory if we find it's necessary to have good perf on those older browsers (and thread safety is not difficult because it's all synchronous).\r\n * **In a web worker (background thread) on more up-to-date browsers**. The .NET/JS interop will need to work by serializing any data that is being transferred rather than passing pointers [1].\r\n\r\nThis will be advantageous because then, even if your .NET code does something that locks up the CPU (such as a GC cycle), the UI will remain perfectly smooth (e.g., during animations or scrolling, or while the user is typing quickly into a textbox).\r\n\r\nThe existing UI update mechanism is designed around transferring batches of minimal diffs from .NET to JS, so it shouldn't be hugely difficult to have it express those diffs as serialized data rather than pointers into the WASM memory space. We'll have to be careful around things like event handling to ensure that the asynchrony can't result in inconsistency of behaviour versus the synchronous single-threaded model. For example, we will need to force all event delivery to be async as far as the JS side is concerned, even in the non-worker-thread case.\r\n\r\n*[1] Strictly speaking, we could also do it with shared memory on even newer browsers that support SharedArrayBuffer. But if we can get satisfactory perf without this, it would be better to serialize because it would mean fewer combinations of browser scenarios, and saves us having to deal with potentially complex thread-safety concerns on the .NET .NET trimmer statically analyzes your project and removes any unused code. In Blazor we use the .NET trimmer to significantly reduce the publish size of Blazor WebAssembly apps. However, we don't currently use the .NET trimmer to its fullest potential. We currently configure the trimmer in a partial mode, which only trims assemblies that are explicitly marked as trimmable. This typically means that the app assembly itself and many dependencies are not trimmed. This is a conservative setting that optimizes for maintaining functionality over reducing app size. \r\n\r\nThe default trim mode for the .NET trimmer is to trim everything. This is the mode used by the .NET Native AOT workloads.Analyzers provide warnings if there are code paths in the app that are not safe to trim. Given how sensitive web apps are to download size and load time, it seems like doing full trimming should be the goal for Blazor.\r\n\r\nEnabling support for full trimming also is a potential solution to enabling a [single project model for Blazor Web Apps](#49079) that target both server and browser. When you multitarget a project, everything in the project is built for both targets unless you indicated otherwise. This is problematic for browser scenarios because you may potentially bring in dependencies, components, and code into the browser targeted build that are only needed on the server. However, if we could enable full trimming *and* indicate to the trimmer which components are setup to render on WebAssembly, then the browser build could be aggressively trimmed to remove any unwanted code and dependencies.\r\n\r\nEnabling support for full .NET trimming typically means removing any dynamic code path that are based on reflection. We would need to make Blazor apps trimmer friendly by removing this code using techniques like source generators. For example, in Blazor we use reflection as part of the component discovery process and in the render tree builder code generated by the Razor compiler. We're already working on enabling [component discovery through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/48767). We also have on our backlog to [handle component parameters through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/29550). There may be other related work items as well.\r\n\r\nThere is also ecosystem impact of enabling full trimming by default. Many .NET libraries are not setup for trimming and would potentially need to be updated. It will take some time to work through these issues with the Blazor community. Certain features also simply wouldn't work with full trimming. For example, dynamically loading dependencies at runtime that are not known statically. For backwards compatibility, app developers can configure the trimmer to not trim assemblies that are not yet trimmer friendly. We'd need to understand better all the cases that get impacted by full trimming and ensure we provide a reasonable user experience for addressing by @SteveSandersonMS] This issue was originally reported by @verdie-g as follows below the line. On investigation the problem is that C# has added a new syntax that doesn't work in Razor.**\r\n\r\nThe Razor compiler allows arbitrary C# code within `@{ ... }` blocks. Unfortunately this means it allows the use of local functions in a way that confuses the parsing logic, causing it to use the wrong `__builder` instance. Example:\r\n\r\n```razor\r\n\u003cFluentTreeView\u003e\r\n@{\r\n    RenderTree(0, 3);\r\n\r\n    void RenderTree(int depth, int maxDepth)\r\n    {\r\n        if (depth \u003e= maxDepth)\r\n        {\r\n            return;\r\n        }\r\n\r\n        \u003cFluentTreeItem Text=\"item\"\u003e\r\n            @{ RenderTree(depth + 1, maxDepth); }\r\n        \u003c/FluentTreeItem\u003e\r\n    }\r\n}\r\n\u003c/FluentTreeView\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nHere, the child content of `FluentTreeItem` should be compiled as a `RenderFragment` that acts on whatever `RenderTreeBuilder` is passed in. But because of C# scoping rules, the `RenderFragment` actually acts on the `__builder` captured from its parent context, so it is simply corrupting the output instead of doing something useful.\r\n\r\nPossible solutions:\r\n\r\n1. We could ask for the Razor compiler block the use of local functions inside `@{ ... }` specifically. However that's probably impractical because Razor doesn't parse the contents of `@{ ... }`.\r\n   * Perhaps it is achievable as an analyzer that acts on the code *after* the Razor compiler has generated it.\r\n2. We could do something in the runtime to detect more generally any cases where the wrong `RenderTreeBuilder` is invoked. For example if the runtime set an \"rendering in progress\" flag on it before it starts rendering and synchronously unsets that flag at the end of rendering, then it would have caught this case because child components are rendered afterwards (not recursively), so when the child is rendered it would see it's trying to write to a builder that does not have the \"rendering in progress\" flag set.\r\n   * Drawback: how do we even check if this flag is set? We would **not** check it as part of each rendering instruction. There's plenty of evidence that rendering perf is sensitive to that kind of thing (and we can't just check it in development either).\r\n   * Possible solution: instead of just setting a flag, actually null out the referencing to the underlying buffer (storing it in some other field to be swapped back later). Then if anyone tries to write to the builder while it's not marked as rendering-in-progress, they will get a `NullReferenceException` instead of corrupt output. Web Component during its initialization (for example, inside `connectedCallback`), the following error is thrown:\n\n\u003e Error: Assertion failed - heap is currently locked\n\u003eat mr (blazor.web.js:1:158963)\n\u003eat Object.beginInvokeDotNetFromJS\n\nThis happens in a Blazor WebAssembly project.The same approach works fine in a .NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid app.\n\nI'm aware that calling .NET from JS during component initialization isn't considered a good practice, but invoking .NET methods would help a gradual migration of a legacy web app to Blazor and MAUI. The goal is to integrate Blazor as a backend facade while preserving the existing UI for now, enabling the team to write new code in Blazor moving forward.\nThe documentation does not appear to impose any restriction that prevents from using this to handle JS calls:  [Link to docs.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/blazor/javascript-interoperability/call-dotnet-from-javascript?view=aspnetcore-9.0#invoke-a-static-net-method)\n\n## Minimal repro repo\n[https://github.com/alexuaua/BlazorDotNetInteropDemo](https://github.com/alexuaua/BlazorDotNetInteropDemo)\n\n## Steps to reproduce\n1. Clone the repo.\n2. Run the project and switch to the Counter page.\n3. Open the browser console.\n4. Observe the `heap is currently locked` error (only) during initialization  of the web component.\n\n## Expected behaviour\nThe JS-to-.NET interop call should succeed (as it does in MAUI Blazor), or there should be a documented workaround for such use cases. Alternatively, the documentation should clearly explain the restrictions on using DotNet.invokeMethodAsync in Blazor WebAssembly apps.\n\n## Actual behaviour\nThe interop call fails due to what appears to be a race condition.\n\nDeferring the call using `setTimeout` (i.e. placing the call later in the stack) resolves the issue, this workaround is even shown in community resources like [Blazor University](https://blazor-university.com/javascript-interop/calling-dotnet-from-javascript/calling-static-dotnet-methods/). \n\nThat said, it would be **very helpful if**:\n- The official documentation explicitly described this race condition and recommended patterns for `DotNet.invokeMethodAsync` in component scenarios.\n- Blazor could provide a way to queue interop calls that are attempted during initialization - would be helpful for migration projects where modifying component logic is non-trivial.\nUnless I’m missing something, the tasks performed in the demo do not require synchronous execution. Blazor WebAssembly’s rendering engine is based on its own component lifecycle and does not track or wait for hydration of external DOM elements, such as those created by Web Components.\n\nThis issue blocks a real-world migration scenario where we cannot immediately rewrite all UI in Blazor. Summary\r\nMark the `IApplicationBuilder.UseWebAssemblyDebugging()` extension (in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server`) as obsolete and stop emitting it from our project templates. Modern IDEs (Visual Studio, VS Code) launch the debug proxy directly. This does mean that the legacy in-browser (Ctrl+Alt+D) will no longer be supported.\r\n\r\n## Background\r\n- `UseWebAssemblyDebugging()` is defined in `src/Components/WebAssembly/Server/src/WebAssemblyNetDebugProxyAppBuilderExtensions.cs`. It maps `/_framework/debug` and uses `DebugProxyLauncher` to start the browser debug proxy (`BlazorDebugProxy/BrowserDebugHost.dll`) for the legacy Chromium/Firefox in-browser experience.\r\n- Related configuration that only exists to support this path:\r\n  - The `inspectUri` value in `launchSettings.json` (`.../_framework/debug/ws-proxy?browser={browserInspectUri}`). This is present in test assets but **not** in the shipping templates.\r\n  - `NO_PROXY` handling and the `/_framework/debug` endpoint, both internal to the middleware/launcher.\r\n- The IDE-driven debugger launches the debug proxy directly and does not depend on this middleware.\r\n\r\n## Customer impact\r\nUsage of the legacy in-browser debugging path appears low. The strongest signal is #61559 (Apr 2025), where browser debugging was broken out of the box on recent Chromium versions for roughly a month; it drew only 11 distinct commenters and no upvotes, and overall issue volume for this path is very small. We may still receive some complaints from users who rely on browser-only debugging (e.g. without Visual Studio, or in Firefox), so we should be sensitive to that in messaging.\r\n\r\n## Proposed changes\r\n1. **Obsolete the API** — Add `[Obsolete]` to `WebAssemblyNetDebugProxyAppBuilderExtensions.UseWebAssemblyDebugging`, using the next diagnostic ID (`ASPDEPR011`) and a new `AspNetCoreDeprecate011Url` entry in `src/Shared/Obsoletions.cs`. Update the public API baseline files (`PublicAPI.Shipped.txt` / `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt`).\r\n\r\n   Obsoletion message:\r\n   \u003e `\"UseWebAssemblyDebugging is obsolete and should be removed along with any inspectUri configurations. Blazor WebAssembly debugging is now launched directly by Visual Studio and Visual Studio Code.\"`\r\n\r\n2. **Remove from the Blazor Web App template** — Remove `app.UseWebAssemblyDebugging();` (guarded by `#if (UseWebAssembly)`) from:\r\n   - `src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/BlazorWebCSharp.1/Program.cs`\r\n   - `src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/BlazorWebCSharp.1/Program.Main.cs`\r\n\r\n   Collapse the now-redundant `#if (UseWebAssembly || IndividualLocalAuth)` / `#if (UseWebAssembly)` conditionals accordingly, and update template baseline/snapshot tests.\r\n\r\n3. **Standalone Blazor WebAssembly template** — Verified no change needed: `ComponentsWebAssembly-CSharp` is client-only and does not reference `UseWebAssemblyDebugging` or `inspectUri`.\r\n\r\n4. **Resolve the internal caller** — `src/Components/WebAssembly/DevServer/src/Server/Startup.cs` calls `UseWebAssemblyDebugging()`. Suppress the new obsoletion warning there (with a justifying comment) so the repo continues to build.\r\n\r\n## Related work\r\n- Companion issue: Deprecate the IMPORTANT: Comments are subject to validation constraints enforced by the MCP server - maximum 65536 characters for the complete comment (including footer which is added automatically), 10 mentions (@username), and 50 links.
